cards.front: An {{c1::allele}} is one version of a gene.
cards.quote: An allele is one version of a gene.

cards.front: In a pea plant, the pair of alleles it carries for a gene, such as Pp, is its {{c1::genotype}}.
cards.quote: P is the purple allele and p the white one. The pair is the genotype.

cards.front: The {{c1::phenotype}} is the trait you can observe or measure, such as flower color.
cards.back: It can also be chemical, such as whether a body makes an enzyme.
cards.quote: The phenotype is the trait you can observe or measure; it can be chemical, such as whether a body makes an enzyme.

cards.front: A {{c1::dominant}} allele (capital letter) shows its trait when one copy is present.
cards.quote: A dominant allele (capital letter) shows its trait when one copy is present.

cards.front: In the pea flower-color gene, when does the recessive allele p show its trait?
cards.back: Only when both copies are recessive (pp).
cards.quote: A recessive allele (lowercase letter) shows its trait here only when both copies are recessive.

cards.front: Homozygous means the two alleles match (PP or pp); {{c1::heterozygous}} means they differ (Pp).
cards.quote: Homozygous means the two alleles match (PP or pp); heterozygous means they differ (Pp).

cards.front: What happens to the two alleles of a gene during meiosis, and what is this called?
cards.back: They separate into different sex cells. This is the law of segregation.
cards.quote: During meiosis, the two alleles separate into different sex cells. This is the law of segregation

cards.front: A Pp pea plant passes on P or p with equal chance. Why is this not truly a coin toss?
cards.back: Nothing is tossed. Meiosis physically separates the two alleles, so each sex cell gets one of them, about half carrying P and half p.
cards.quote: This resembles a coin toss, but nothing is tossed: meiosis physically separates the alleles.

cards.front: Two purple parents can have a white offspring. How can a recessive allele stay hidden for a generation and then show up again?
cards.back: A heterozygous (Pp) parent is purple but still carries p, and passes it on with a 50 percent chance. An offspring that gets p from both parents is pp, so white.
cards.quote: so a recessive allele can stay hidden for a generation and then show up again.

cards.front: In peas, a Pp plant is crossed with a pp plant. What fraction of the offspring are expected to be white, and why?
cards.back: One half. Pp makes P and p sex cells equally, and pp makes only p, so half the equally likely boxes are Pp (purple) and half are pp (white).
cards.quote: A Pp plant makes P and p sex cells. A pp plant makes only p sex cells.

cards.front: For two Pp pea plants crossed, what are the expected genotype ratio and phenotype ratio of the offspring?
cards.back: Genotypes 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp. Phenotypes 3 purple : 1 white, because PP and Pp both look purple.
cards.quote: The genotypes come out 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp (1:2:1), and the phenotypes 3 purple : 1 white (3:1), because PP and Pp both look purple.

cards.front: Two Pp pea plants have three purple offspring in a row. What is the chance that their fourth offspring is white?
cards.back: 1 in 4, the same as for every offspring. Each offspring begins with a new pair of sex cells, so earlier offspring do not change the chance.
cards.quote: Each offspring begins with a new pair of sex cells, so the chance of pp is still 1 in 4.

cards.front: Two Pp pea plants produce four offspring. What is the chance that all four are purple?
cards.back: Each offspring is purple with chance 3/4, so 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 = 81/256, about 32 percent.
cards.quote: All four offspring could be purple: 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4, about 32 percent.

cards.front: Does a Punnett square for two Pp parents guarantee that 4 offspring will be 3 purple and 1 white? What should real counts do instead?
cards.back: No. It gives the probability of each outcome, so real counts scatter around its ratios instead of matching them exactly.
cards.quote: A Punnett square gives the probability of each outcome, so real counts of offspring scatter around its ratios instead of matching them exactly.

cards.front: A RrYy plant makes four sex-cell types (RY, Ry, rY, ry). When is each type 1 in 4?
cards.back: Only if getting R or r does not affect getting Y or y. This is the law of independent assortment.
cards.quote: Each type has a 1 in 4 chance only if getting R or r does not affect getting Y or y.

cards.front: Two RrYy pea plants are crossed. What phenotype ratio is expected for round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green?
cards.back: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, out of 16 equally likely boxes.
cards.quote: Grouped by phenotype: round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1

cards.front: Two RrYy pea plants are crossed. What fraction of offspring are expected to be RrYy, and why?
cards.back: 1/4. Rr is 1/2 of offspring and Yy is 1/2, and the genes assort independently, so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. This is 4 of the 16 boxes.
cards.quote: Each box is one of 16 equally likely outcomes, because the four sex-cell types are equally likely.

cards.front: Two RrYy pea plants are crossed. Ignoring color, what share of offspring are expected to be round, and why?
cards.back: 3/4. Shape sorts independently of color, so shape alone follows the one-gene 3:1 (9 + 3 = 12 of 16 boxes are round).
cards.quote: Because shape sorts independently of color, each gene still gives its own one-gene 3:1.

cards.front: Two genes sit close together on one chromosome. A student expects a 9:3:3:1 ratio from a dihybrid cross. What should you say, and why?
cards.back: The ratio can depart from 9:3:3:1. The 9:3:3:1 square assumes independent assortment, and genes close together on one chromosome are linked.
cards.quote: Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and can depart from 9:3:3:1.

cards.front: In Mendel's flower-position experiment, 207 of 858 plants had flowers at the tip (recessive). What was the recessive share, and how does it compare with the 3:1 prediction?
cards.back: 207 ÷ 858 × 100 is about 24.1 percent, close to the 25 percent a 3:1 ratio predicts.
cards.quote: Recessive share = recessive count ÷ total.
cards.section: Test the model against Mendel’s counts

cards.front: Across Mendel's seven traits in the second generation, about what share of plants or seeds showed the recessive trait, and what does it show about the model?
cards.back: About 24 to 26 percent in every trait, close to the 25 percent a 3:1 ratio predicts. The model fits the counts well.
cards.quote: For seven traits, Mendel let hybrid plants fertilize themselves and counted the second generation.
cards.section: Test the model against Mendel’s counts

cards.front: Mendel counted 556 seeds in his dihybrid cross: 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow, 32 wrinkled green. A 9:3:3:1 ratio predicts about 313, 104, 104 and 35. Which category was furthest from its prediction?
cards.back: Round green, 108 seen versus about 104 predicted, about 4 seeds off. The other three were off by 2, 3 and 3.
cards.quote: In his dihybrid experiment, Mendel counted 556 seeds from 15 plants: 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green.
cards.section: Test the model against Mendel’s counts

cards.front: Two Pp plants are crossed in a simulation. One group plants 10 offspring and another plants 1,000. Which share of white is likely to land nearer one in four, and why?
cards.back: The 1,000. Each offspring has a 1 in 4 chance of white, so small samples scatter widely, while larger samples usually come closer to the predicted ratio.
cards.quote: Cross two Pp plants. Predict how many of 10 will be white, then plant 10.
cards.section: Explore: cross two plants and count the offspring

cards.front: You have a purple pea plant that is PP or Pp. Which cross makes a hidden p allele easiest to detect, and what outcome tells you each genotype?
cards.back: Cross it with a white plant (pp), a test cross. A PP parent gives only P, so all offspring are purple. A Pp parent gives p half the time, so about half the offspring are white.
cards.quote: Cross the purple plant with a white plant (pp). This is a test cross.

cards.front: In the test cross of an unknown purple plant with a white plant (pp), how many offspring should you grow? Give the chance of all-purple offspring if the parent is Pp, for 2 offspring and for 20.
cards.back: If the parent is Pp, each offspring is purple with chance 1/2. For 2 offspring, 1/4. For 20, (1/2)^20, under one in a million. So grow at least 20: all purple then very likely means PP.
cards.quote: the chance of 20 purple in a row (no white plants) is one-half multiplied 20 times: under one in a million.

cards.front: A test cross of a purple pea plant with a white plant (pp) gives one white offspring among many purple ones. What can you conclude about the purple parent, and why?
cards.back: It is Pp. A PP parent can only give P, so no offspring could be white; one white offspring needs a p from the purple parent.
cards.quote: Even one white offspring means the purple parent is Pp. All purple in a large sample means it is very likely PP.

cards.front: A student says Mendel's 224 white among 929 plants (24.1 percent) shows the 3:1 model is wrong, because it is not exactly 25 percent. Evaluate this claim.
cards.back: The claim is weak. A Punnett square gives chances, so real counts scatter around its ratios. A result near 25 percent in a large sample of 929 fits the model well.
cards.quote: The square organized those chances; it did not promise offspring.
